name: Tape Programming
description: There is a programming language in which every program is a non-empty sequence of " < " and " > " signs and digits. Let's explain how the interpreter of this programming language works. A program is interpreted using movement of instruction pointer (IP) which consists of two parts. Current character pointer (CP); Direction pointer (DP) which can point left or right; Initially CP points to the leftmost character of the sequence and DP points to the right. We repeat the following steps until the first moment that CP points to somewhere outside the sequence. If CP is pointing to a digit the interpreter prints that digit then CP moves one step according to the direction of DP. After that the value of the printed digit in the sequence decreases by one. If the printed digit was 0 then it cannot be decreased therefore it's erased from the sequence and the length of the sequence decreases by one. If CP is pointing to " < " or " > " then the direction of DP changes to "left" or "right" correspondingly. Then CP moves one step according to DP. If the new character that CP is pointing to is " < " or " > " then the previous character will be erased from the sequence. If at any moment the CP goes outside of the sequence the execution is terminated. It's obvious the every program in this language terminates after some steps. We have a sequence s 1 , s 2 , ..., s n of " < ", " > " and digits. You should answer q queries. Each query gives you l and r and asks how many of each digit will be printed if we run the sequence s l , s l + 1 , ..., s r as an independent program in this language.
input_specification: The first line of input contains two integers n and q (1 ≤ n , q ≤ 10 5 ) — represents the length of the sequence s and the number of queries. The second line contains s , a sequence of " < ", " > " and digits ( 0..9 ) written from left to right. Note, that the characters of s are not separated with spaces. The next q lines each contains two integers l i and r i (1 ≤ l i ≤ r i ≤ n ) — the i -th query.
output_specification: For each query print 10 space separated integers: x 0 , x 1 , ..., x 9 where x i equals the number of times the interpreter prints i while running the corresponding program. Print answers to the queries in the order they are given in input.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 238D — Tape Programming [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
